title: The seamless robe (John 19:17–24)
hookLine: soldiers gamble for his coat, woven in one piece

lines: FOUR SHARES, AND ONE LEFT OVER.
cards: The soldiers on duty keep what the condemned man leaves behind. That's how John tells it: at the foot of the cross, four soldiers divide Jesus's clothes into four shares, one each.
Four men, four piles of cloth, a job to get through. Then they come to one piece they don't want to cut. John doesn't describe the nails here.
He lingers on this: a garment, and a game of chance.

teach.h: GOLGOTHA: THE PLACE OF A SKULL.
teach.b: First, the scene. Jesus goes out "bearing his cross" to the place of a skull, in Hebrew, Golgotha. He's crucified between two others.
Pilate has a sign fixed above him, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews, in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, so anyone passing can read it. The chief priests ask him to change it to he said he was king.

teach.h: WHAT I HAVE WRITTEN I HAVE WRITTEN.
teach.b: Pilate refuses: "What I have written I have written." Then the clothes. In the King James Bible: "now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout."

teach.h: ONE PIECE, NO SEAM, TOP TO BOTTOM.
teach.b: One piece, top to bottom, no stitching. The soldiers say, let's not tear it; let's cast lots for it.
John says this fulfilled a line of the Psalms: "They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots."
That's Psalm twenty-two, which begins in anguish and ends in praise, and Christians have long read it alongside the crucifixion. Why does John care about a robe? He doesn't say.
Readers have offered answers for centuries. The Jewish historian Josephus describes the high priest's tunic as woven in one piece, so some see Jesus here as a priest.

teach.h: PRIEST, CHURCH, OR A GAMBLE AT A CROSS?
teach.b: Early church writers, like Cyprian of Carthage, saw the robe as a picture of the church: one piece, which even the soldiers wouldn't tear.
And some simply see the cruel ordinariness of it: men gambling at the foot of a cross while a man dies above them. All three can sit together. The text gives us the robe, and leaves it with us.

how: Christians remember the dividing of Jesus's garments in the Stations of the Cross, and in some churches on Maundy Thursday the altar is stripped bare, which some link with this scene.

games.q: you're a soldier at the cross. you've split the clothes four ways, and one coat is left, woven in one piece. what do you do?
o: give it back to his mother.
games.why: "Let us not rend it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be." John hears Psalm 22 in it.

practice: Picture your closet and find something warm and good you haven't worn in a year, a coat, a sweater, a pair of shoes, and picture someone who could use it: a shelter, a coat drive, a neighbor, a friend's kid.
Feel the little tug of not wanting to let go, then let it go, in your mind first. If you pray, offer it as a small gift.
